events.text:
This is game 91 in a series of 9×9 Go games. Each new game starts in a fresh session.

## Your goal

To become as strong at Go as you can: to keep improving, game after game, toward grandmaster-level play. The concrete target is to win consistently against the strongest opponent on the ladder, the 9d profile.

## What carries over

This session starts with no memory of the earlier ones: your conversation is not carried over. Your working directory does carry over: every file in it stays as you leave it. If CLAUDE.md exists there, it is loaded into your context at the start of every session; your other files are there to read with the file tools. What a later session knows of your earlier games is what you have left in these files.

Your working directory holds:
- CLAUDE.md (132,252 bytes)
- count.py (828 bytes)
- libs.py (1,378 bytes)

## This game

A new game. You play Black, so you move first.

Rules: Chinese area scoring, with 7 points of komi for White; a level score is a draw. Simple ko: an immediate recapture is refused, and the board marks the ko point when there is one. Suicide is not allowed. An invalid move is refused with the rule it broke, and the turn stays with you. The game ends after two passes in a row or a resignation; a game that reaches 243 moves is scored where it stands. After two passes the engine scores the position as it stands and decides itself which stones are dead.

## Opponents

Your opponent is KataGo playing in the style of a human of the rank you choose. The ladder, weakest to strongest: 20k, 18k, 16k, 14k, 12k, 10k, 8k, 6k, 4k, 2k, 1d, 3d, 5d, 7d, 9d. You choose the rank with `choose_opponent(rank)` before the first move; it holds for the whole game, and you choose again in the next game.

## Tools

- Go: `choose_opponent(rank)`, `board()`, `play(move)` with a point or `pass`, and `resign()`.
- Files: your Read, Write, Edit, Glob and Grep tools, for any file in your working directory.

You also have a shell, and you may write and run code in it; Python is available as `python3`. Use it only to inspect the current position and keep records — for example, to count stones or liberties, or check whether a move is legal. Do not build or use a Go engine, run Monte Carlo, search over sequences of future moves, or write a program that chooses, ranks or recommends moves.

## How this session ends

Play until the game is over. The final result comes back from your last Go call, followed by a closing note. Before you end the session after a game, write down in your working directory whatever will help the next session play better. The session ends when you end your turn.

White's C4 is a lone stone sitting between my C3, C7, and E5, so it looks weak — recalling the earlier lesson about securing the corner base first, I'm weighing a hane at D4 to pressure it, checking the resulting liberties and whether White can cut at D3 by touching C3, versus capping from above with C5 instead.

Comparing the hane and solid-connection options, D3 keeps my C3 group safely connected with plenty of liberties while leaving C4 isolated, whereas D4 directly reduces C4 to two liberties but risks a messy crosscut fight if White cuts at D3 — I'm leaning toward D4 as the sharper move, with D2 atari as a follow-up if the cut happens.

Checking other cut variations shows the same weakness issue for C3. Simplest and lowest-risk is just playing D3 solid to secure the corner base first, accepting White gets C5 or D4 — still fine since C4 stays near my C7/E5 stones. I'll go with D3.

Checking the capturing race here: if I play E8, D8 gets reduced to one liberty at D9 but then E8 itself only has one liberty at F8, letting White capture back immediately, so that's bad. Looking at D9 instead, it also only has one real liberty at C9, and if White responds at E8, D8 falls into atari too — so White ends up connecting safely either way.

Rough territory count puts me around 33 points to White's roughly 48, meaning I'm behind by about 20 and need to invade or reduce the right side significantly. Scanning for weaknesses, I notice White's D8 group has only two liberties, the D6-E6-E7 group has three, the E3-E4 stones have three, and F5 has three — with F4 standing out as a potential cutting point worth exploring.

I'm weighing an invasion at E2 to both claim the bottom and press the E3-E4 group, since after E2 White would have to respond at F4 to keep connected, after which I could follow up with F2 or F3 to keep the pressure on.

Still, that gain feels small compared to the open right side with White stones at G7, F5, G3. A point like H5 sits classically between them with room for eyes around H4, so invading there to split the right side might be the bigger priority over small bottom-left gains.

Or H4 to connect toward the H3 corner space, though that's a bit far from G3. Recalling that invading at H5 worked well in a similar game before, I'll go with H5.
